question: In multiplayer, how is speaking time split between the host and everyone else — one voice carrying the video, or talk genuinely shared?
pole_low: Host narrates nearly everything; other players are heard only in short replies
pole_high: Talk time is shared roughly evenly; partners open lines, own scenes, and land punchlines the host reacts to
why: Round 2 showed the same creator at both poles: Jesse Gillett narrates 100% of his solo video but roughly half of his co-op one, while OMB Gaming directs everything himself in both formats. An avatar playing with kids needs a ruled answer for how much of the talk it keeps.
evidence_needed: Speaker-attributed transcripts (or dialogue-structure coding) for 3+ multiplayer videos per creator: share of lines and scene-ownership per speaker.

question: After a phase ends, who gets to reveal the hidden information — the host performing a reveal, or the participants disclosing themselves?
pole_low: Participants reveal themselves in dialogue; discoveries are mutual and unstage-managed
pole_high: The host stages and narrates every reveal (admin tours, result announcements) as a set segment
why: OMB Gaming's post-round reveal tour is a signature ritual where the host performs everyone's hiding spots; Jesse's co-op discoveries happen inside dialogue. Reveal privilege decides who owns the best moment of a group game.
evidence_needed: Group-format videos: code each reveal event by who discloses it and whether it is a produced segment or spontaneous dialogue.

question: When an ally tricks or betrays the host mid-scene, is it treated as a rule break to punish, or as prized content to celebrate?
pole_low: Betrayal is punished, reversed, or edited out; the agreed fiction is restored
pole_high: Betrayal is celebrated on mic as the best beat of the video
why: Jesse Gillett's partner secretly mined his ship and attacked under cover of a rescue, and both tricks got delighted reactions. For a family-audience avatar this sets the tone for every trick a kid coach will inevitably try.
evidence_needed: Multiplayer segments containing an in-fiction trick or betrayal: code the host's immediate reaction (punish/restore vs celebrate/replay) across creators.

question: How much of the plan is spoken aloud in advance — kept as a genuine surprise for the other players, or fully narrated so the audience (and opponents) know what is coming?
pole_low: Plans stay hidden until execution; even the audience learns by watching
pole_high: Plans are fully narrated in advance to audience and players alike, as briefings or open taunts
why: OMB briefs his whole raid in character where everyone can hear; Jesse announces his ramming plan to his opponent and it becomes shared analysis. Plan audibility decides whether suspense comes from secrecy or from watching a known plan collide with reality.
evidence_needed: Code consequential plans in multiplayer videos: was the plan stated on mic before execution, and could the affected players hear it?

question: Between rounds, who changes the setup — the host resetting everything unilaterally, or changes proposed and agreed with the players on mic?
pole_low: Host resets unilaterally: same rules, new round, no negotiation
pole_high: Changes are proposed, seconded, and agreed with players in dialogue before the next round
why: Jesse's ship-swap between rounds is agreed in one exchanged line; OMB restarts rounds by decree with the rules restated. For Coach Player this is the multiplayer mirror of the nudge-ruling question: who authors the next attempt.
evidence_needed: Inter-round segments in multiplayer videos: count setup changes by origin (host decree vs negotiated) per creator.

question: Does the host use production-level tools the in-scene characters should not have (admin reveal, spectator view, cheats) secretly, or openly on camera as part of the show?
pole_low: Production tools are used off-camera or never acknowledged; the fiction stays seamless
pole_high: Production tools are named and used openly on camera as their own segment
why: OMB calls his admin view his cheats out loud and tours the map with it; the honesty is the bit. An agent that will run games for kids needs a ruled stance on showing its own machinery.
evidence_needed: Segments where admin/spectator tools are visibly used: is the tool named, joked about, or hidden? Sample across hosted-event creators.

question: When the game itself breaks — a crash, a glitch, a lost round — how much is it narrated as part of the show versus treated as an interruption to apologise for or edit around?
pole_low: Breakage is minimised: apologised for, cut, or papered over with a declared result
pole_high: Breakage is absorbed as content: narrated, joked about, and converted into a promise or a next episode
why: Jesse's final round was decided by the game crashing, and he turned it into the ending plus a rematch promise instead of declaring a winner. Our avatar will face broken sessions with kids watching; the response is character.
evidence_needed: Videos containing a genuine technical failure: code the creator's handling (apology/edit vs narrate/absorb) and whether the outcome was declared anyway.

question: At the debrief, where does the credit go — to the host's skill, or outward to the players, the commenters, and the community?
pole_low: Credit flows to the host: their plan, their skill, their win
pole_high: Credit flows outward: teammates, opponents, commenters and community are named as the reason it worked
why: OMB closes by crediting the supporting crew and the hiders; Jesse credits a commenter for his video's premise and his partner for the best beats. Credit direction is a warmth and trust signal a young audience reads instantly.
evidence_needed: Closing/debrief segments across creators: count credit statements by recipient (self vs others) and whether any are specific or generic.
